introduction: Yesterday we celebrated all the saints in glory; today the Church remembers all the faithful departed. We pray for our own dead, for those no one remembers, and for all who are being made ready to see God face to face. The readings do not hide the grief of loss. Lamentations speaks of a soul bowed down, yet holds on to hope: the Lord's mercies are "new every morning." Paul proclaims that death is swallowed up in victory, and Jesus calls all who are weary to come to him for rest.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, our hope is in the Lord, who is merciful and gracious. Let us pray for the living and the dead.
intentions: For the Church: that she may always proclaim the hope of the resurrection, and keep alive the ancient practice of praying for the dead. Let us pray to the Lord.

For all the faithful departed, especially those who died this year and those who have no one to pray for them: that, purified of every stain of sin, they may come into the light of God's presence. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the members of our families and our parish who have died: that the Lord who knew them by name may welcome them into his peace. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who mourn: that the Lord, who has compassion on his children as a father does, may console them and give them hope. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may live each day ready to meet the Lord, trusting in his mercy rather than our own merits. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Father of mercies, you remember that we are dust, yet you call us to share your life for ever. Hear our prayers for the living and the dead, and bring us all together into your kingdom. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Mercies new every morning
reflection.body:
The first reading comes from the Book of Lamentations, written after the fall of Jerusalem. Its author knows grief from the inside: "My strength has perished, along with my expectation from the LORD." Many of us have said something like that beside a grave. Then, in the middle of the lament, the writer turns: "This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope." What he recalls is not a feeling but a fact about God: "his mercies don't fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness."

That is why the Church prays for the dead. The Catechism teaches that those who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, undergo a final purification before entering the joy of heaven, and that our prayers, above all the Eucharist, help them (Catechism 1030-1032). Praying for the dead is not doubting God's mercy; it is trusting it enough to keep asking.

Paul looks further ahead, to the day of resurrection, when "this mortal must put on immortality." He can almost taunt death: "Death, where is your sting?" The victory is not ours to win. It is given: "thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."

In the Gospel, Jesus speaks to everyone who carries a load too heavy for them: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest." Grief is one of those burdens. He does not ask us to stop mourning; he asks us to bring our mourning to him.

Today, name your dead before God, one by one. Visit a grave if you can, or light a candle. And let the psalm teach you how God sees them and us: "He remembers that we are dust", and he has never once forgotten our names.
